title: How Sam Bankman-Fried Actually Lost $8 Billion
hook: At twenty-nine, Sam Bankman-Fried was worth twenty-six billion dollars on paper. A year later, eight billion dollars of his customers' money was simply gone -- and almost everyone had believed him right up until the end.
body:
Sam Bankman-Fried graduated MIT in 2014, joined the trading firm Jane Street Capital, then quit in 2017 to found Alameda Research, a crypto trading firm, out of a rented Berkeley apartment. In 2019 he co-founded the exchange FTX with MIT classmate Gary Wang; Caroline Ellison (another Jane Street alum) ran Alameda, and Nishad Singh led FTX's engineering. A January 2022 funding round valued FTX at $32 billion, backed by Sequoia, SoftBank and Temasek; Bankman-Fried's own stake was worth as much as $26 billion on paper, and Forbes ranked him the richest person under 30 in America. FTX ran a marketing campaign fronted by Larry David (Super Bowl LVI, February 2022), Tom Brady, Gisele Bündchen and Steph Curry, and Bankman-Fried gave roughly $40 million to political campaigns that cycle. At Bankman-Fried's direction, engineer Gary Wang built a software exception letting Alameda Research -- nominally just another customer account -- run an effectively unlimited negative balance (reported as roughly $65 billion of credit capacity) without the margin calls any other account faced. Through that backdoor, roughly $10 billion in FTX customer deposits moved to Alameda over time, backed in large part by FTT, a token FTX had created itself. On November 2, 2022, CoinDesk published a leaked Alameda balance sheet showing its holdings were heavily FTT. On November 6, Binance CEO Changpeng Zhao announced Binance would liquidate its FTT holdings, triggering a bank run: FTX saw roughly $6 billion in withdrawal requests within 72 hours, halted withdrawals on November 8, and a rescue deal with Binance collapsed by November 9. On November 10, Bankman-Fried posted a public apology thread ("I'm sorry... I f---ed up, and should have done better"); on November 11, FTX, Alameda and roughly 130 affiliated companies filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, and John J. Ray III -- who had overseen the Enron bankruptcy -- was installed as CEO. Ray's bankruptcy filing called it "a complete failure of corporate controls." Bankman-Fried was arrested in Nassau, the Bahamas, on December 12, 2022, the night before he was scheduled to testify before Congress; the next day, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams announced an 8-count indictment, calling it "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history." Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 and cooperated with prosecutors; Nishad Singh pleaded guilty soon after. At trial (Oct 3-Nov 2, 2023, before Judge Lewis Kaplan), Ellison testified Bankman-Fried directed her to use customer funds to cover Alameda's losses, fund investments, real estate and political donations, and said she felt relief when it collapsed because she "didn't have to lie anymore." A jury convicted Bankman-Fried on all seven counts on November 2, 2023. On March 28, 2024, Judge Kaplan sentenced him to 25 years in federal prison and ordered $11 billion in forfeiture. Caroline Ellison was sentenced to 2 years on September 24, 2024. This is what the DOJ's indictment and plea agreements, SDNY press releases, and contemporaneous trial reporting say happened.
